newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rwanda leader defends country's justice system.
newsitem.headline: Rwanda leader defends country's justice system.

text.p: Rwandan vice-president and de facto leader Major-General Paul Kagame said on Monday that his country was improving its justice system, now under international criticism.
"Trials are better than no trials," Kagame told a news conference in Tokyo. "We are better with the trials (that are going on) and (we are) in the process of bettering them."
At least 18 people have been sentenced to death in Rwanda courts for involvement in the 1994 genocide of an estimated 800,000 Tutsis and Hutu moderates by Hutu troops, militiamen and mobs.
Kagame arrived in Japan on Sunday for a six-day visit.
He said that Rwanda was forced to build a justice system from scratch after the 1994 genocide destroyed the country's legal structure.
"The criticisms will serve to make us work harder and better the justice system, which was non-existent for the last two years," Kagame said.
Kagame also said he was ready to welcome back the 100,000 Rwandan refugees staying near Kisangani in eastern Zaire which the U.N. agencies wanted to repatriate.
"Our country remains open to all, even if they may have committed crimes," Kagame said.
Many of the Rwandan Hutu refugees, who fled their country three years ago after the victory of Tutsi rebels, are fearful of returning home because they could be blamed for the 1994 genocide.
Kagame called on Japan and other nations to offer aid to Rwanda, which he said has moved from a state of emergency to that of economic development.
Last week, Amnesty International said most trials in Rwanda for genocide and crimes against humanity were unfair.

The human rights group said defendants in Rwanda were presumed guilty unless proved innocent and lawyers were reluctant to become involved due to a climate of hostility towards those accused in the killings.
